99.title: Covering the eyes
99.hook: hands circle the candle flames, then cover the eyes while the blessing is said
99.howItsDone: Shabbat candles are lit shortly before sunset on Friday; the person lighting often circles their hands over the flames, covers their eyes, says the blessing, and many add quiet words of their own before uncovering their eyes to look at the light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, erev Shabbat: Friday's cooking, cleaning and washing. Your line was get ready for a guest. Did you clear your surface? Now the guest arrives. Day ninety-nine.

Most people have a place where they get ten seconds alone. The car in the driveway, engine off, before you go inside. The stairwell at work. A locked bathroom door at a loud party. You put your face in your hands, and for a moment nobody needs anything from you. In many Jewish homes, those ten seconds come at the same time every week. Friday, just before sunset, the candles are lit. The hands circle the flames, then come up over the eyes, and the person lighting stands in the dark of their own palms while the blessing is said. And often they stay there a little longer than the blessing takes. Today: what happens behind the hands.
screen: `TEN SECONDS ALONE.` → `HANDS CIRCLE THE FLAMES.` → `A LITTLE LONGER THAN THE BLESSING.`

segments.voice: On day four you met the two flames, and the reason for the hands: once the blessing is said, Shabbat has begun, so people light first, cover their eyes, bless, and then look. Today, stay behind the hands a little longer. The blessing itself is short. It thanks God, who commanded the lighting of the Sabbath lamp. But in many homes the hands don't come down right away. People speak quietly, in their own words. For centuries this was one of the few moments in the week that belonged to the woman of the house, and people wrote prayers for it. From the sixteen hundreds on, Jewish women in central and eastern Europe used small books of personal prayers in Yiddish, called tkhines, and many include one for the candles: for a husband's livelihood, for a sick parent, for children who would grow up to love learning. They weren't in the official prayer book. They were in the language of the kitchen. And the rabbis took their model of personal prayer from a woman. In the first book of Samuel, Hannah, longing for a child, prays at the sanctuary in Shiloh. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The priest Eli watches her and decides she's drunk. The Talmud reads the scene the other way: this is how to pray. The heart turned toward the words, the lips moving, the voice kept low. Watch someone at the candles and you'll often see exactly that. Lips moving. No sound. Then the hands come down, and the week is over.
screen: `ON DAY FOUR: LIGHT, COVER, BLESS.` · `THE HANDS STAY UP A LITTLE LONGER.` · `TKHINES: PRAYERS IN THE KITCHEN'S LANGUAGE.` · `HANNAH: LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` · then, large: `ONLY HER LIPS MOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cover your eyes and breathe three times. If you have a candle and it's safe, you can light it first. If not, just picture one. Bring your hands up and rest them gently over your eyes. Breathe in, and out. That's one. Let the week's noise go quiet. Two. Think of someone you'd hold in your heart at a candle, if you pray, or simply wish well if you don't. Three. Then lower your hands slowly, open your eyes, and look at the first thing you see as if it were new. The bell holds the time.
Covering the eyes. At Shabbat candles: light, circle the hands, cover the eyes, bless, and then look, as if the blessing came first.
Your line: eyes closed, the week ends. Tonight, before you move into the evening, cover your eyes for three breaths and let one part of the day be finished. Day ninety-nine.

100.title: Shalom Aleichem
100.hook: the Friday night song welcomes angels; the Talmud says two walk you home (Shabbat 119b)
100.howItsDone: On Friday night, after returning from synagogue and before Kiddush, many families stand around the table and sing Shalom Aleichem, each of its four verses three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, covering the eyes at the candles: light, cover, bless, then look. Your line was eyes closed, the week ends. Day one hundred. A hundred days. That's worth a breath on its own.

Picture the walk home on a Friday night. The streets are quieter than usual. Somebody's coming back from synagogue with a child on their shoulders. Maybe it's cold, maybe it's warm and you can hear other families' dinners through open windows. You open your door, and the candles are already burning, the table is set, and before anyone sits down, the family stands around the table and starts to sing. Not to each other. To guests nobody can see. Today: Shalom Aleichem, peace be upon you.
screen: `THE WALK HOME ON FRIDAY NIGHT.` → `THE CANDLES ARE BURNING.` → `A SONG FOR GUESTS NO ONE CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Shalom aleichem means peace be upon you. It's also an everyday greeting, the way people say hello in Hebrew and Yiddish. But on Friday night it's a song, and it's sung to angels. The idea comes from a story in the Talmud. Two ministering angels, it says, walk a person home from synagogue on Friday night, one good and one bad. When they arrive, if the candles are lit, the table is set and the beds are made, the good angel says: may it be like this next Shabbat too. And the bad angel has no choice but to answer amen. If the house is dark and nothing's ready, it goes the other way around, and the good angel has to say amen. It's a story about habit, really: the way you welcome this week shapes the next. The song itself is much younger than the story. It's usually traced to the Kabbalists of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and it has four short verses, each sung three times. Welcome, angels of peace. Come in peace. Bless me with peace. Go in peace. Some people have asked, reasonably, why you'd tell angels to leave. One answer is simple courtesy: they walked you home, and now you can let them go. Another is that the family is about to sit down together, and some moments are just for the people at the table. Families sing it to many tunes, fast and slow. Some hold hands. Some sing it once, quietly, alone. It turns an ordinary doorway into the place where the week's peace comes in.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum a song as you walk in your door. Practice it now. Settle, and breathe. Picture the door you'll walk through next: home, work, a friend's place. Picture your hand on it. Now pick a tune, any tune that feels like peace to you, and hum a little of it, even under your breath. Picture walking through that door humming, and imagine two quiet companions walking in with you, noticing what kind of place you've made. The bell holds the time.
Shalom Aleichem. Peace be upon you: a greeting, and the Friday night song that welcomes the angels of peace home.
Your line: angels walk you home. Today, when you walk in your door, hum something first, and leave the place a little readier than you found it. Day one hundred.

101.title: Blessing the children
101.hook: hands on a child's head: may you be like Ephraim and Manasseh, or like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah
101.howItsDone: On Friday night, many parents place their hands on each child's head, bless sons to be like Ephraim and Manasseh and daughters like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, and add the priestly blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shalom Aleichem: the song for the two angels who walk you home. Your line was angels walk you home. Did you hum at the door? Day one hundred one.

Think of the last time someone put a hand on your head. Probably when you were small. A parent checking for a fever, a grandparent at a doorway, a coach after a game. It's one of the oldest gestures there is, and one of the gentlest. On Friday night in many Jewish homes, after the song for the angels and before the wine, the children line up, or wriggle, or pretend they're too old for this. And a parent puts both hands on each child's head and says the same few words people have said for centuries. Today: blessing the children.
screen: `A HAND ON YOUR HEAD.` → `CHILDREN LINE UP, OR WRIGGLE.` → `THE SAME WORDS FOR CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: You've met the words already, back in Genesis. Old Jacob, near the end of his life, blesses his two grandsons, Joseph's sons, and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." So that's what's said over sons. Why these two, and not Abraham or Moses? One answer the tradition gives: Ephraim and Manasseh were the first brothers in Genesis who didn't fight. After Cain and Abel, Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Joseph and his brothers, here are two who got along, even when the younger was put first. Another answer: they grew up in Egypt, far from home, and still stayed who they were. For daughters, the words are: may God make you like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, the four mothers of the people, each with her own hard and brave story. Then, in many homes, comes the blessing the priests gave in the Temple, from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Parents say it with their hands resting on the child's head. Some whisper something personal after, about the week, a test, a friendship. Some bless grown children over the phone. Some grandparents bless grandchildren. It's short. It takes maybe thirty seconds a child. And for many kids, it's one of the things they remember most about Friday nights, long after they leave home: every week, no matter what happened, someone put their hands on my head.
screen: `AS EPHRAIM AND AS MANASSEH.` · `THE FIRST BROTHERS WHO DIDN'T FIGHT.` · `SARAH, REBEKAH, RACHEL, LEAH.` · `THE PRIESTS' BLESSING.` · then, large: `THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone you love, aloud or silently. Settle, and breathe. Bring one person to mind: a child, a parent, a partner, a friend. Picture their face. If they were here, picture your hands resting gently on their head. If you pray, you can say the old words for them, the LORD bless thee, and keep thee. If you don't, simply wish them well, clearly, in your own words. Stay with them for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Blessing the children. On Friday night, hands on each child's head: like Ephraim and Manasseh, like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, and the priests' blessing.
Your line: hands on heads. Today, tell one person you love what you hope for them, even in a text, even in one sentence. Day one hundred one.

102.title: Kiddush
102.hook: a cup of wine or grape juice declares the day holy, remembering creation and the Exodus
102.howItsDone: On Friday night, before the meal, someone at the table lifts a cup of wine or grape juice and recites Kiddush, beginning with Genesis 2:1–3, and everyone then takes a sip.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessing the children: Ephraim and Manasseh, the four mothers, and hands resting on a head. Your line was hands on heads. Day one hundred two.

At a wedding, there's a moment when someone taps a glass, everyone stands, and a toast turns an ordinary evening into an occasion. Same room, same people. But now it's official: this night matters. On Friday night, in Jewish homes all over the world, there's a moment like that at the table. Someone lifts a full cup of wine or grape juice, the room gets quiet, and they say words that turn a Friday evening into something else. Today: Kiddush.
screen: `SOMEONE TAPS A GLASS.` → `NOW IT'S OFFICIAL.` → `A FULL CUP ON FRIDAY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kiddush means making holy, from the same root as kadosh, holy. It comes from the commandment, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." The rabbis asked: how do you remember a day? And they answered: you say so, out loud, over a cup of wine. Wine, because it's what people drink at a celebration. Grape juice works too, and many families use it. If there's no wine at all, the blessing can be said over the challah. On Friday night, Kiddush begins with the last lines of the creation story in Genesis: "And the heaven and the earth were finished, and all the host of them." Then God rested on the seventh day and blessed it. Then comes the blessing over the fruit of the vine, and then a longer blessing that names two reasons for the day. Shabbat is a remembrance of creation, the world God made and finished. And it's a reminder of the Exodus, leaving Egypt. Why the Exodus? Because in Deuteronomy the Sabbath commandment says: remember that you were a slave in Egypt. Slaves don't get days off. Free people do. So every Friday night, one cup holds two memories: the world was made, and we were set free. Customs vary. Some stand, some sit. Some hold the cup in the palm of the hand. Afterward, everyone takes a sip, often from little cups poured from the big one. It's short, maybe a minute. But it does what the toast does at a wedding. It says it out loud: this time is different.
screen: `KIDDUSH: MAKING HOLY.` · `REMEMBER IT OVER WINE.` · `CREATION, AND LEAVING EGYPT.` · `FREE PEOPLE REST.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY, TO KEEP IT HOLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: raise any drink and say one sentence of thanks. Water is fine. Coffee is fine. Pick up whatever is near you, or picture it. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your life that you didn't make but get to enjoy, and one way you're more free than you once were. Then lift the cup a little, and say one sentence of thanks, out loud if you can. If you pray, you can offer it to God. Then drink slowly. The bell holds the time.
Kiddush. Making holy: a blessing over wine or grape juice that declares Shabbat holy, remembering creation and the Exodus.
Your line: make it holy out loud. Today, before one meal or one moment, say out loud that it matters, even in one sentence. Day one hundred two.

103.title: Two loaves
103.hook: two loaves recall the double manna; they stay covered while the wine is blessed
103.howItsDone: At Shabbat meals, two loaves of challah sit covered on the table during Kiddush; then the cover is removed, the blessing over bread is said, and the challah is often salted, torn and shared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kiddush: one cup for two memories, creation and freedom. Your line was make it holy out loud. What did you say out loud? Day one hundred three.

Walk into almost any bakery in a Jewish neighborhood on a Friday morning and you'll see them stacked up: shiny, golden, braided loaves, soft inside, a little sweet. People buy two. Always two. Take them home and put them on the Friday night table, and there's another odd detail: they're covered with a cloth, often embroidered, sometimes made by a child at school, while the wine is blessed. Two loaves, under a cloth, waiting their turn. Today: challah.
screen: `A FRIDAY MORNING BAKERY.` → `ALWAYS TWO.` → `COVERED, WAITING THEIR TURN.`

segments.voice: Why two? Go back to the manna, a few days ago on this path. Every morning in the wilderness, bread from heaven, enough for one day. But on the sixth day, the Torah says, the people gathered twice as much, a double portion, because nothing would fall on Shabbat. So the Shabbat table has two loaves, lechem mishneh, double bread, to remember the double manna. Two loaves say: there was enough, even for the day we didn't gather. Now the name. Challah in the Torah is actually the portion of dough set aside for the priests. Many bakers still pinch off a small piece of dough and set it aside before baking, with a blessing, and the whole loaf came to be called by that name. The braids are a custom, not a law. They're common among Ashkenazi Jews, whose families came from central and eastern Europe; other communities bake flat breads or round loaves, and on the New Year many make them round. Why the cloth? There are several answers. One says the manna lay between two layers of dew, one below and one above, so the bread sits on a board and under a cover. Another answer is so gentle it sounds like a children's story, and it's told that way too: normally bread's blessing comes first, so the bread is covered so it won't be embarrassed while the wine goes ahead of it. A tradition that worries about the feelings of a loaf is a tradition teaching you to notice everybody's feelings. Then the cover comes off, the blessing is said, the bread is often sprinkled with salt, and it's torn and passed around.
screen: `TWO LOAVES FOR THE DOUBLE MANNA.` · `CHALLAH: THE PORTION SET ASIDE.` · `BRAIDED, ROUND OR FLAT.` · `COVERED, LIKE DEW OVER MANNA.` · then, large: `THERE WAS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cover your bread before you eat. At your next meal, if there's bread, or anything at all, lay a napkin over it for a moment first. Try it in your mind now. Settle, and breathe. Picture the food under the cloth. Think about where it came from: the field, the bakery, the hands, the truck. Think of one way you had enough this week, even when you didn't do the gathering. Then picture lifting the cloth, slowly, like opening a gift. The bell holds the time.
Challah. The Shabbat bread, two loaves for the double manna, covered while the wine is blessed, named for the piece of dough set aside.
Your line: two loaves, enough. Today, when you eat, notice one thing you have enough of, and say so. Day one hundred three.

104.title: A woman of valor (Proverbs 31:10–31)
104.hook: many homes sing Eshet Chayil on Friday night to honor the women of the house
104.howItsDone: In many homes, Eshet Chayil (Proverbs 31:10–31) is sung at the Friday night table before Kiddush, often by a husband to his wife or by the whole family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, challah: two loaves for the double manna, covered while the wine is blessed. Your line was two loaves, enough. Day one hundred four.

Think of the person in your life who keeps everything running and almost never hears about it. The one who knows where the birth certificates are, remembers everyone's allergies, and fixes the thing before anyone notices it's broken. When was the last time someone said, out loud, in front of everybody, what they do? In many Jewish homes on Friday night, someone at the table does exactly that, in a song whose words come straight from the Bible. Today: Eshet Chayil, a woman of valor.
screen: `THE ONE WHO KEEPS IT RUNNING.` → `SAID OUT LOUD, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` → `ESHET CHAYIL.`

segments.voice: It's the last chapter of the book of Proverbs, and it opens, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "A woman of valour who can find? For her price is far above rubies." Eshet is woman, and chayil is a strong word. It means strength, ability, even an army. Valor is a good translation. This isn't a delicate portrait. The woman in the poem buys a field, plants a vineyard, runs a business, stays up late, gets up before dawn, feeds her household, opens her hand to the poor, and speaks with wisdom and kindness. "Strength and dignity are her clothing," it says. The poem is an acrostic: its twenty-two verses begin with the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, from alef to tav, as if to say, praise her with every letter there is. In many homes it's sung on Friday night, often by a husband to his wife, sometimes by the whole family. The Kabbalists who made it part of the Friday night table also read it about Shabbat itself, or about God's presence, the Shekhinah, and some read it about the Torah. Jews read it in different ways today. Some sing it to wives and mothers. Some to every woman at the table. Some feel its ideal is a heavy one to live up to, and choose other readings, or sing it to honor someone they've lost. The book of Ruth calls Ruth a woman of valor too, using the same Hebrew words. And the poem ends with a line about public praise: "let her works praise her in the gates." Don't keep it private. Say it where people can hear.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise someone in your home out loud. First, find the words. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone you live with, or someone you love who's far away. Walk through their week the way the poem walks through hers. What did they carry? What did they do that nobody thanked them for? Pick one specific thing, not a general compliment. Shape it into one clear sentence. Then decide when you'll say it, where they can hear it, maybe where others can too. The bell holds the time.
A woman of valor. Eshet chayil, the poem that ends Proverbs, sung on Friday night to praise the strength of a woman's work.
Your line: say the praise. Today, say your sentence out loud to the person who earned it, and if you can, say it in front of someone else too. Day one hundred four.

105.title: What isn't done, and why (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2)
105.hook: thirty-nine kinds of creative work, linked to building the tabernacle, are set aside
105.howItsDone: Observant Jews refrain from the thirty-nine categories of melacha from sundown Friday until Saturday night, preparing food, lights and other needs in advance; other Jews keep some of them or set aside work in their own ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman of valor, praise sung out loud on Friday night. Your line was say the praise. It's the end of a week at the Friday table: candles, the angels' song, the children's blessing, Kiddush, challah and Eshet Chayil. Day one hundred five.

Here's a puzzle people bring up about Shabbat. You can carry a heavy table across the living room and it's fine. But in many observant homes, you won't flip a light switch, and you won't write a two-letter word on a sticky note. That sounds backward. Moving furniture is hard. Writing is easy. If Shabbat is about rest, why is the easy thing off the table? The answer is that the Hebrew word usually translated as work doesn't mean effort at all. Today: melacha.
screen: `CARRY A TABLE: FINE.` → `WRITE TWO LETTERS: NOT TODAY.` → `WORK ISN'T EFFORT.`

segments.voice: Melacha means creative work: the kind that makes something, changes the world, or puts your stamp on it. The Torah says don't do melacha on Shabbat, but it barely says what melacha is. One of the only examples it gives, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." So how did the rabbis define it? They noticed that right after that verse, the Torah turns to building the mishkan, the tabernacle, the one we closed camp two with. Shabbat and the mishkan, side by side. So the rabbis said: whatever kinds of work it took to build the mishkan, those are the kinds of work you set aside on Shabbat. You can build a holy place in space six days a week. On the seventh, you stop, and live in holy time. The Mishnah lists them, forty less one, thirty-nine. They read like a tour of a workshop in the ancient world: sowing, plowing, reaping, grinding, kneading, baking. Shearing, dyeing, spinning, weaving, sewing. Writing two letters, erasing. Building, tearing down. Kindling a fire, putting one out. Carrying from one domain to another. Everything later rabbis decided about modern life, from cars to electricity, grows out of those thirty-nine, and Jewish movements apply them differently. Orthodox Jews keep them in detail. Many Conservative and Reform Jews keep some, or choose their own ways to rest. But the idea underneath is the same, and it's a surprising one. For one day, you stop being the one who shapes the world, and let the world be. The not-doing is the practice.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one kind of work to skip. Settle, and breathe. Go through your day in your mind and notice the ways you make and change things. Typing, buying, cooking, fixing, editing, posting. Pick one. Just one, and small. Decide on a time this week when you'll set it aside for a few hours. Not because it's hard, but because it's yours. Then picture that stretch of time: your hands still, the world going on without your edits. The bell holds the time.
Melacha. Creative work, not effort: thirty-nine kinds, drawn from building the mishkan, set aside on Shabbat.
Your line: not doing is a practice. Today, skip your one kind of work for an hour, and notice what fills the space. Day one hundred five.
